rationale: No panel dissent is in the packet. The judgment changed at the claim level while the case verdict holds at well_supported. Since the incumbent the ledger admitted Rostain 2024 (AMZ-E073–E076: the Upano occupation that built the platforms ran from about 500 BCE to 300–600 CE, with Huapula reoccupation 800–1200 CE) and Achmatowicz 2018 (AMZ-E072 on the new claim AMZ-C065; AMZ-E077 as weak context on AMZ-C017). The anchored-is-not-evidenced rule now governs the grading: six featured claims held on their anchors alone with no admitted evidence record — AMZ-C019, C020, C021, C022, C023 and C029 — are regraded unresolved at low confidence (the incumbent held C019 well_supported and C020–C023 provisionally_supported), and the article tells each as what the ledger holds, never as a finding. AMZ-C016 has neither anchor nor record of its own; it is graded on the admitted evidence for its named dependencies and that basis is disclosed in its reasoning. The featured set grows by two: AMZ-C061, because the dated Upano chronology decides how far the erasure argument in C022 can discount contact-era palaeoecological negatives — the erased signal was a millennium old, not four centuries — and AMZ-C065, an independent published route (geography, not manuscripts) to Carvajal's credibility, graded on an abstract-only record. Weakest links now list every anchor-only featured claim beside C017 and C015; the load-bearing set is unchanged. The steelman adds the geographic-route convergence, marked as the proponents' reading of an unread body. The crux order seats the two new research items (the Laureano headcount, the erasure calibration) after the corridor test, the matrix surveys and the witness table; no item is settled, so researchStatus is empty. The article adds an erasure-chronology passage, a pointer to the 1650 headcount item, and the anchor-only disclosures, and compresses the fisheries, connectivity and comparator passages to hold length near the incumbent's; what the added lines buy is that a reader can now see which propositions the record holds as observations and which only as statements. The prose treats the same five accounts the field lists, one section each in the map and one prediction each in the closing tests.
article:
In the summer of 1542, a starving Dominican friar floated down a river no European had ever descended, keeping notes. Gaspar de Carvajal was the chaplain of Francisco de Orellana's accidental expedition — a few dozen men in a makeshift brigantine who had set out to find cinnamon and ended up crossing South America by water. What he recorded was not wilderness. [His chronicle describes populous riverbank settlements running for leagues, storehouses of food, travelled roads leading inland, fine ceramics, and organized polities — alternating with stretches he reports as empty]{claim=AMZ-C001}.

For most of the twentieth century, educated opinion held that he was lying, or at best embellishing. The Amazon of the textbooks was a “counterfeit paradise”: soils too poor, protein too scarce, floods too brutal for anything beyond small shifting villages. An eyewitness account of crowded riverbanks was an embarrassment to be explained away — a friar magnifying marvels for patrons back home. And later travelers, arriving a century and more afterward, found mostly what the textbooks predicted: forest, and silence.

This case is about what happens when the instruments catch up with the argument — and about the discipline required to say precisely how much of the friar's world they have found.

## Five ways to read the friar

Set the serious readings side by side, because the evidence below sorts among them unevenly.

- **Invention.** Carvajal made up or grossly inflated a world that never existed; the Amazon could not have supported it. This predicts no large contact-era settlements along his route and no independent witnesses to them.
- **A murdered world.** Carvajal described faithfully what he saw; epidemics, slave raids, missions, and flight destroyed and scattered it before the next visitors arrived. This predicts dense contact-horizon archaeology in his populated reaches and documented collapse mechanisms operating specifically on riverbanks.
- **The garden Amazon.** The whole basin — interfluves included — was densely peopled and intensively managed, by many millions. This predicts intensive-use signals nearly everywhere the soils are cored.
- **The mosaic.** Dense, engineered corridors and hotspots set in a lightly occupied forest matrix; Carvajal is qualitatively honest and numerically unreliable. This predicts strong signals near rivers and bluffs and weak ones in the deep interfluves.
- **The modest skeptic.** Real societies, but smaller than the eyewitnesses imply; Orellana travelled the richest corridors, archaeology looks where it can see, and the emptier later Amazon partly records a modest reality rather than only a collapse. This predicts that population models fall apart under their own assumptions and that the negative record holds up under better sampling.

The first reading has not survived. The other four are live, and the question of proportion — how much corridor, how much matrix — is what separates them.

## The account, and its two texts

Before weighing Carvajal against archaeology, there is a problem inside the text itself. His chronicle survives in two main manuscript families, and they do not say the same things. [The most famous numbers — 50,000 warriors, 10,000, 8,000, villages four and five leagues long — appear in the Medina/Muñoz branch but not in Oviedo's version, which preserves the same crowded world with one figure of about 5,000 warriors]{claim=AMZ-C002}. Whatever else is true, the extreme figures are textually unstable in a way the qualitative picture is not. A serious reading of Carvajal was never “believe him” or “dismiss him”; it is: trust the kind of world he described, refuse his arithmetic. Which figure sits in which witness deserves a passage-by-passage collation this record does not yet hold; the branch comparison it relies on is a geographer's, verified from a scanned copy.

And his description does not stand alone. [A Portuguese named Diogo Nunes had raided the same Machiparo province four years before Orellana, and the ten surviving accounts of the 1560 Ursúa expedition independently describe dense settlement, maize stores one chronicler called infinite, long straight roads “in the manner of the Incas of Peru, except for the walls,” and ceramics of famous quality]{claim=AMZ-C003} — on the same reaches, from witnesses writing for different crowns who were not copying one another. None of them repeats Carvajal's giant numbers. All of them repeat his world. A 2018 study takes a third route to a similar verdict, checking the chronicle's geographic reference points and league distances against the river, and [judges the manuscript a trustworthy historical source]{claim=AMZ-C065}; this record has read only its abstract, which says nothing about the figures. Two limits travel with all of this: fortifications and organized warfare are not among the features the witnesses share, and the route itself is still argued — [one river in Carvajal's itinerary is glossed in the recovered literature with an explicit question mark]{claim=AMZ-C024}, a point held here on its anchor alone.

## What the lasers found

{plate:IMG-AMZ-P01}

The modern turn begins when researchers notice geometric ditches emerging from deforested pasture in the Brazilian state of Acre — and accelerates when LiDAR, which strips the canopy off the terrain model, goes looking under the trees. The survey program led by Martti Pärssinen and Alceu Ranzi has published its reckoning: [flying 4,430 kilometers of laser lines, it documented 432 earthworks where satellite imagery had found a fraction of that, and projects roughly 24,000 to 30,000 monuments across a 183,000-square-kilometer cultural region]{claim=AMZ-C004} — more, for one corner of the basin, than a 2023 basin-wide model predicts remain undiscovered in all of Amazonia.

{plate:IMG-AMZ-P02}

Three honesty notes belong here. First: the study proposes a peak population of 1.25 to 3 million people — but [that figure is an assumption engine, resting on how many earthworks were in use at once and on about 300 people per monument, and the paper's own alternative reading of the same data yields roughly 250,000 to 600,000]{claim=AMZ-C005}. The monuments are certain; the census is a model. Second, and larger: the Aquiry florescence is dated to roughly AD 100–300. It is decisive evidence that Amazonian environments could carry monument-building societies — and weak evidence about what Orellana saw fourteen centuries later. This case refuses to spend ancient grandeur as contact-era corroboration. Third: the 2023 model, built from earthworks known before this LiDAR campaign, estimates 10,272 to 23,648 undiscovered earthworks across all 6.7 million square kilometers of Amazonia and places nearly all of its highest-probability cells in a 94,713-square-kilometer rectangle over Acre — roughly half the Aquiry area. The two studies define “earthwork” differently and use different data and estimators, so the comparison contradicts nothing; it does show that published earthwork totals differ several-fold between models, and that only a survey chosen blind to promise, stratified by predicted probability, can tell which is calibrated.

**Transparency.** The 2026 study's funding statement reads, in its own words: “The project and data collection were funded by a grant from E. Jhong (USA).” That is this site's founder. The Athanatos Foundation, with which he is associated, is acknowledged for administrative assistance. Readers should know this — and should notice that it is exactly why this case presents the paper's population claim at its most assumption-exposed, not its most headline-friendly.

What matters for Carvajal is the archaeology whose dates overlap him. [An 1,800-kilometer arc of the southern rim was occupied by earth-building societies in fortified villages around AD 1250–1500]{claim=AMZ-C006}, with its own population model — half a million to a million — stated as a model that depends on every site being lived in at once. And [several major settlement systems ran into the contact era and beyond: the Belterra Plateau sites near Santarém from about AD 1300 to seventeenth-century colonization, complete with dark earths, ponds, and trodden roads; Marajó's Cacoal site to 1650; and Upper Xingu settlements inhabited until about 1770, their circular-plaza layouts matching the villages living Kuikuro communities build today]{claim=AMZ-C011}. That last point deserves its own sentence: some of this is not a lost world at all, but a continuous one — collapsed in numbers, unbroken in pattern. The caution is geographic: Santarém, Marajó, and the Xingu are the lower Amazon and its southern tributaries, not the Machiparo and Omagua reaches where Carvajal's most famous passages sit.

## Engineered ground

{plate:IMG-AMZ-P03}

The subsistence question — *what could they all have eaten?* — was always the strongest scientific objection, and it now has at least one direct answer. [In the Llanos de Mojos, the Casarabe culture ran intensive year-round maize agriculture on a savannah it had replumbed: drainage canals for the wet season, farm ponds for the dry, documented by phytoliths in the fields themselves]{claim=AMZ-C007}. More broadly, [dark earths, raised-field complexes, forest islands, and orchard-like concentrations of domesticated trees around archaeological sites record long human engineering of Amazonian ground]{claim=AMZ-C008}.

{plate:IMG-AMZ-P04}

The savannah's waters were engineered too, and “they couldn't have gotten enough protein” was for decades the respectable core of the impossibility argument. Here the record is uneven in an instructive way. The paper on the San Joaquín floodplains reports [zigzag weirs and straight causeways crossing the savanna, most of the hundreds of detected ponds within thirty-five meters of one, and postulates that the V-shaped structures served to concentrate fish as the floods receded]{claim=AMZ-C019} — but this ledger holds that only on the paper's anchor; no evidence record from it has yet been admitted, and the claim is graded accordingly. The diet, by contrast, is in the ground and in the record: [one settlement's refuse holds more than seventeen thousand fish bones, including dry-season species like lungfish that persist in small waters — year-round aquatic harvest, fifty kilometers from the big river]{claim=AMZ-C026}. One site's refuse is an existence proof, not a census. But the specific claim the old skepticism rested on — that the interfluves could not feed sedentary people through the year — now has a documented counterexample in bone, and in maize. Note the calendar: the Casarabe world ends around 1400, a century and a half before Orellana. It answers the impossibility argument; it does not describe 1542.

Engineering is not a census, and this case keeps the distinction structural. [The raised fields of the Bolivian lowlands, dated carefully, show intermittent construction and use — plausibly flood-risk works built where nothing else would do — not a permanent breadbasket]{claim=AMZ-C009}. And the domesticated-forest signal carries a first-class qualifier: five post-Columbian centuries have shaped the modern forest too, and the formal critique arguing they did most of the shaping is part of this record. A second study finds that [across 1,676 forest plots, 53 of 79 domesticated tree species track the modelled probability that earthworks are present]{claim=AMZ-C033} — corroboration, but from inside the same research network, using the same species list, and open to the same post-Columbian confound. The record counts it once, not twice.

## How many people?

The honest answer to the famous question is that the published numbers — one million, five, six, ten — are not competing measurements. They are competing models, and several descend from the same assumptions. The field's most influential estimator said so himself: [Denevan publicly rejected the habitat-density method behind his own 5.1–6.8 million figure, while still judging “at least 5 to 6 million” reasonable on other grounds]{claim=AMZ-C012}. A number can outlive the death of the argument that produced it; a reader deserves to know when that has happened.

What the aggregate evidence does support: [radiocarbon proxies for the whole biome fit a population growing logistically toward carrying capacity right up to European arrival]{claim=AMZ-C015} — no sign, at basin scale, that Amazonian societies were already dying out on their own before the caravels. The authors' own caveats govern: the proxy tracks relative change, its terminal dip is attributed to sampling bias compounded by post-contact collapse, and “carrying capacity (however high)” says nothing about how high.

## The disappearance

If Carvajal described a real world, where did it go? The documented answer, where colonial records permit counting, is brutal and specific. [In the Napo–Aguarico province, an estimated 49,000–51,000 people in the early contact period became about 6,000 by 1700 — an 88 percent collapse; neighboring Mainas lost roughly two-thirds — through differing regional mixtures of epidemics, slave raids, missionization, forced labor, revolt, and flight]{claim=AMZ-C010}. Note the mechanism list: people did not only die in place. They were taken, gathered into missions, and they fled — most, the record says, from exposed locations along the major rivers. The same paper is anchored here for a further proposition — that [in sparse lowlands epidemics commonly “faded out,” and it was the raids and the missions that kept reintroducing them]{claim=AMZ-C023} — which the ledger holds on that anchor alone, without an admitted evidence record; it is plausible and ungraded, not established. A riverbank empty in 1690 is not evidence it was empty in 1542; it may be evidence of everything that happened in between.

The limit is that these counts come from upper-Amazon provinces with mission records. The Solimões reaches where the dispute actually lives have no equivalent reconstruction, and the reconciliation argument borrows ratios from where the records are. The nearest thing to a mid-century count for Carvajal's Omagua reach — a Franciscan resident's headcount from around 1650 — survives in a 1900 edition whose printed numeral is garbled, and reading the manuscript behind it is one of this case's research items.

## The sparse Amazon

Everything above could be true and the maximalist picture still false, and the negative evidence is part of this case's spine, not an afterthought. [Across 7,363 recorded archaeological sites, distance from a river is the single strongest predictor of pre-Columbian occupation, with the deep interfluves markedly sparser]{claim=AMZ-C013}. And [where scientists have cored the soils of the western and interfluvial Amazon — fourteen regions and counting — most terra-firme profiles show closed-canopy forest with little to no sign of crops, clearing, dark earths, tree enrichment, or recurrent fire]{claim=AMZ-C014}. The skeptics of the garden Amazon are not defending the old impossibility thesis; they are defending proportions. Two modelling papers are anchored here for that position — one reckoning [the famous earthworks and dark earths cover a “limited, albeit impressive” fraction, with humbler site types dominating more than two-thirds of the basin]{claim=AMZ-C020}, the other reported as putting [almost 80 percent of Amazonia at a 0–1 percent chance of holding an earthwork in any given square kilometer, the low-probability country concentrated in the northwest, north, and center]{claim=AMZ-C029} — and both are held on their anchors alone, with no evidence record admitted from either; the ledger knows where the propositions are stated and grades them unresolved until it holds the observation behind them.

The negatives have their own critics, and here too the ledger holds statements rather than records. A formal reply argues that [the “sparse west” rests on some three hundred soil cores in five clusters — about a cubic meter of sediment standing in for two million square kilometers]{claim=AMZ-C021}; a palaeoecological study of the Upano Valley in Ecuador reports that [forest recovery largely erased the pre-Columbian signal even though the later colonial signal survived]{claim=AMZ-C022}, so that a negative would mean less the older the activity. Both are anchor-only in this record. What the record does hold is the Upano chronology from the excavating team: [the builders of its platforms and roads occupied the valley from about 500 BCE to between 300 and 600 CE]{claim=AMZ-C061}, with [some mounds reoccupied between 800 and 1200 CE]{claim=AMZ-C062}. The erased signal, in other words, was a thousand years old or more. Whether a signal four centuries old — the age of a riverbank depopulated in the 1600s — would also be gone is exactly what the erasure argument needs and does not yet have; a research item below proposes to measure the decay against sites with dated abandonments. And the site database that produces the river-distance gradient inherits the fact that archaeologists survey where they can reach. The case logs all of these biases rather than choosing one.

## What would decide it

Each live account makes a prediction the ledger can eventually check.

- **The corridor test.** Classify every reach of the 1541–42 route as populated or empty from the manuscripts alone, model the route's uncertainty, then compare contact-horizon (AD 1400–1650) archaeology in his populated reaches against matched controls. The murdered-world and mosaic readings predict a strong match; the modest skeptic predicts that his populated reaches are real but no denser than other bluff-and-channel settings; invention predicts nothing there at all.
- **Promise-blind surveys.** LiDAR and gridded coring across interfluvial blocks chosen without regard to archaeological promise, with controls for whether the method could have detected occupation. The garden Amazon predicts interfluve densities approaching riverine ones; the mosaic predicts a real but low matrix; the modest skeptic predicts near-zero outside a few hotspots.
- **The witness table.** A passage-by-passage collation of the manuscript branches. If the qualitative bedrock turns out to be branch-specific too, Carvajal's rehabilitation weakens; if only the figures are, it hardens.
- **The 1650 headcount.** Read the Biblioteca Nacional manuscript behind the garbled 1900 edition to fix how many men a resident friar found on the Omagua reach a century after Carvajal. Tens or hundreds would mean the corridor was near-empty by mid-century, a dated witness for the murdered world; low thousands would mean a province of a thousand or more households still standing in 1650, moving the collapse's timing and size.
- **Erasure calibration.** Score anthropogenic indicators in soil profiles beside sites with archaeologically fixed end dates — Upano, Casarabe, Belterra, Marajó, the Xingu — and plot signal against years since abandonment. If four-century-old signals survive while Upano's millennium-old one is gone, the erasure argument cannot discount contact-era negatives.
- **Stratified LiDAR.** Survey blocks drawn at random within probability strata of the two earthwork models, to see which total is calibrated.
- **Dependency-corrected demography.** Sort every published estimate into its model family and re-derive them under one assumption set, so model families stop masquerading as independent censuses.
- **Middle-Amazon collapse timelines.** Extend province-by-province reconstruction to the Solimões, testing whether documented decline and relocation suffice to turn 1542 into the later silence.

## Where this case lands

[The pre-contact Amazon that survives every filter in this record is a strongly heterogeneous one: substantial populations, engineered subsistence, and settlement systems along favored corridors and hotspots, embedded in a much more lightly occupied forest matrix]{claim=AMZ-C016}. This is a synthesis, not an observation — it carries no evidence record of its own and stands on the corridor archaeology and the river-distance gradient beneath it. Neither the pristine wilderness nor the wall-to-wall civilization survives contact with the evidence; what remains open is proportions, and “heterogeneous” only earns its keep once the matrix density is measured rather than inferred.

How connected was this world? The ledger holds, on its anchor, a linguist's boundary: [regional interaction spheres are well documented — shared ceramic traditions, exchange, stable multilingualism — while the strong version, a continent-spanning Arawak-dominated integration, is assessed as resting on “quite weak” evidence]{claim=AMZ-C025}, a criticism its author limits to the strong version. That is the mosaic again, at the level of politics and language.

And the friar? [Carvajal now looks substantially credible about the qualitative social geography he described, and untrustworthy about his extreme numbers]{claim=AMZ-C017} — a more interesting vindication than the wholesale kind, because it is earned by discounting everything discountable and testing what is left. It is also provisional. The corroboration comes from the same corridors and the same genre of conquest narrative; the contact-horizon settlement systems dated so far lie downstream and to the south of his most famous passages; and the test that would close the question has not been run.

## Credit where the record supports it

One more genealogical fact belongs in the open. [Years before the 2026 results, Graham Hancock's *America Before* devoted seven chapters to the Amazonian discoveries — the Acre geoglyphs among them — and his 2024 series put Pärssinen and Ranzi themselves in front of a mass audience]{claim=AMZ-C018}, at a time when this research was marginal to the mainstream conversation. On this site, outsider status is not evidence — in either direction. Hancock's larger lost-civilization thesis is not what this evidence establishes, and the mainstream's numerical skepticism about Carvajal has been partly vindicated by the manuscript work. But a truthful genealogy records who kept the question alive while the instruments were catching up, and this is such a record.

assessment.synthesis: The thesis graded is the heterogeneous one: substantial sedentary populations, engineered subsistence and settlement systems along favored corridors and hotspots, set in a much more lightly occupied forest matrix, with Carvajal qualitatively credible and numerically unreliable. It is carried from both directions by admitted records. Positively: earthworks at enormous scale (AMZ-E001), fortified southern-rim villages dated AD 1250–1500 (AMZ-E004), settlement systems occupied into the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries at Santarém, Marajó and the Xingu (AMZ-E017, E018, E019), engineered year-round maize and a year-round interfluvial fish diet where the carrying-capacity objection was strongest (AMZ-E014, E022), and independent 1538 and 1560 witnesses converging on the same middle-Amazon reaches Carvajal described (AMZ-E007), with the extreme figures shown to be branch-specific (AMZ-E005). Negatively: the river-distance gradient across 7,363 sites (AMZ-E010) and the thin intensive-use signal in fourteen sampled regions (AMZ-E011) cap the garden-Amazon reading. Demography stays a set of assumption-driven envelopes (AMZ-E002, E009), and the basin-wide comparator (AMZ-E038, E039) shows earthwork totals differ several-fold between models; the tree-species corroboration (AMZ-E040, E041) is from one research network and counts once. This edition regrades six featured claims that the ledger holds on anchors alone with no admitted evidence record — the fisheries infrastructure (C019), the site-type and probability-surface modelling (C020, C029), the soil-core sampling critique (C021), the Upano erasure (C022) and the epidemic fade-out mechanism (C023) — to unresolved. Two consequences follow. The qualifiers that kept the negatives from being read as proof of emptiness are now statements rather than records, so the lightly-occupied half of the thesis rests on E010 and E011 with their own stated limitations, not on a contest between records. And the newly admitted Upano chronology (AMZ-E073, E074) dates the erased occupation to 300–600 CE with reoccupation to 1200 CE, so even if the erasure claim is admitted it speaks to a signal a millennium old, not to the four-century-old signal of a riverbank depopulated in the 1600s; AMZ-R008 is the test. Achmatowicz's geographic-route assessment (AMZ-E072, E077) converges with C017 but is abstract-only and silent on the qualitative-versus-numerical split. Neither invention nor pristine wilderness survives the record; what it cannot yet fix is the matrix density that separates the mosaic from the modest skeptic, or contact-horizon archaeology on Carvajal's own reaches. Sensitivity: the single evidence record whose removal would most change the case verdict is AMZ-E007. Without it the Carvajal leg (C017) falls to weakly supported — every remaining corroboration is archaeological, off his route, or earlier than him — and the founding question's verdict would fall to provisionally supported even though the archaeological mosaic (C016) would stand. On the matrix side AMZ-E010 plays the equivalent role: without it the lightly occupied half rests on the fourteen-region synthesis alone.
assessment.steelman: Every witness who saw the middle Amazon before the epidemics — Nunes in 1538, Carvajal in 1542, the ten Ursúa chroniclers in 1560 — reports the same specific, unglamorous features on the same reaches: stores of maize, long straight roads compared to Inca roads without walls, ceramics of known reputation, dense settlement (AMZ-E007). These witnesses wrote for different crowns and, on the admitted reading, did not copy one another; convergence on mundane detail is what shared exaggeration does not produce, and the one feature that does not converge — the giant warrior counts — is exactly the feature the manuscript branches show to be unstable (AMZ-E005), which is the signature of a truthful observer whose numbers grew in transmission. A scholar working from a different direction, testing the chronicle's geographic reference points and league distances against the river, reads the manuscript as a trustworthy source (AMZ-E072); proponents take that as an independent check on the friar's honesty, though this ledger has read only the abstract. Nothing admitted contradicts the witnesses where they stood: the negative palaeoecology is from interfluves and the west, not from the Solimões bluffs. Where colonial records permit counting, decline of 62–88 percent within a century and a half is documented, by mechanisms — flight from exposed river locations, gathering into missions, slave raids — that empty riverbanks specifically (AMZ-E008); every lower-Amazon settlement system dated so far runs into the seventeenth century or later (AMZ-E017, E018, E019); and the basin-wide radiocarbon proxy grows to the eve of contact with no endogenous crash (AMZ-E020). On this argument the burden lies on the skeptic to explain why corridor eyewitnesses should be discounted when nothing contradicts them where they stood, and this assessment has no record that does so; it holds Carvajal at provisionally supported only because the direct corridor test has not been run and the dated contact-era systems lie off his route.
assessment.whatIsClaimed: That Gaspar de Carvajal's 1542 chronicle describes a real world — populous, organized, road-connected riverine societies along specific reaches of the Amazon; that Amazonian environments could and did support large sedentary populations with engineered subsistence, at scales revealed by LiDAR earthworks, dark earths, raised fields, canals and fish weirs; and that Old World epidemics, slave raiding, missionization and flight destroyed and dispersed that world fast enough that the emptier Amazon met by later travelers records a collapse rather than proving the earlier account false. The version this assessment grades is the heterogeneous one: dense corridors and hotspots embedded in a lightly occupied forest matrix, with Carvajal qualitatively credible and his extreme numbers a transmission artefact.
assessment.whereDisagreementLives: Not over whether complex Amazonian societies existed — earthworks, dark earths, engineered savannas and planned settlements are established beyond argument. The live cruxes are proportion and inference. How representative were the populated corridors of the basin, when river distance is the dominant predictor of known occupation and most sampled interfluves show little intensive modification — while the critiques of that negative sampling, and the erasure argument that would discount it, are held in this ledger on anchors without admitted records? Do population estimates survive their own assumptions, when the largest recent figure falls roughly fivefold under the paper's own alternative reading, the field's most influential estimator rejected his own method, and earthwork totals differ several-fold between predictive models? How much of Carvajal is textual bedrock versus transmission artefact, when the most famous warrior counts sit in one manuscript branch only? And are spectacular but much earlier or geographically distant sites — the Aquiry peak of AD 100–300, Upano ending by 600 CE, the Casarabe world ending around 1400, the lower-Amazon systems — being silently spent as evidence about the reaches Carvajal saw in 1542?
assessment.whatWouldSettleIt: A preregistered Carvajal corridor test: classify his populated and empty reaches from the manuscript witnesses alone, model route and palaeochannel uncertainty, then compare contact-horizon archaeological intensity in his populated corridors against matched controls — before consulting the archaeological layers. Alongside it: promise-blind interfluve surveys with proxy-sensitivity controls to measure the matrix density directly; a synoptic manuscript-witness table separating what every Carvajal branch shares from what one branch carries; the Biblioteca Nacional manuscript reading that fixes the 1650 Omagua headcount; an erasure-decay calibration against sites with dated abandonments, so the Upano argument stops standing in for four-century-old signals; a probability-stratified blind LiDAR sample to calibrate the competing earthwork totals; demographic estimates re-derived under a common assumption set; and province-by-province collapse timelines extended to the Solimões.
assessment.bestConventionalExplanation: The modern skeptical position is not the old ecological-impossibility argument; it concedes major regional societies and argues limits. Orellana travelled the richest corridors — the bluff-and-channel settings where settlement concentrated and where archaeology preferentially looks and preserves — so corroboration there cannot license basin-wide extrapolation. Sampled western and interfluvial palaeoecology shows large areas without intensive cultivation, clearing or soil modification, and predictive modelling over known sites finds the spectacular earthworks and dark earths a limited, if impressive, fraction. The famous population totals are model outputs whose assumptions — site contemporaneity, persons per earthwork, extrapolation domains — do most of the work, and the estimators themselves have said so. Carvajal's extreme figures are textually unstable across manuscript branches, consistent with a truthful observer whose numbers grew in the telling. On this view the mosaic is real but modest: dense hotspots, thin matrix, and a chronicle that is qualitatively honest and numerically unreliable, describing a world that was both smaller than legend and then genuinely destroyed.

components.label: Carvajal's qualitative social geography (C001, C003, C017, C065)
components.note: Independent 1538 and 1560 witnesses converge on the same reaches (E007) and a geographic-route study concurs (E072, abstract only); no contact-horizon archaeology yet on his own reaches, and the corridor test is unrun.

components.label: The numbers: manuscript figures and population totals (C002, C005, C012)
components.note: The extreme warrior counts are branch-specific (E005); the Aquiry and basin totals are assumption envelopes whose authors say so (E002, E009). Established as unreliable counts.

components.label: Monumental earthworks and settlement systems (C004, C006, C011, C061)
components.note: 432 documented earthworks and a regional projection (E001); fortified southern-rim villages AD 1250–1500 (E004); Santarém, Marajó and Xingu systems into the contact era (E017–E019). Chronology caution: Aquiry peaks AD 100–300 and Upano ends by 600 CE.

components.label: Engineered subsistence (C007, C008, C009, C026, C019)
components.note: Year-round maize (E014), year-round interfluvial fishing at one mound (E022), dark earths and domesticated-tree concentration with a post-Columbian confound (E012, E013, E040, E041), intermittent raised fields (E015, E016); the fish-weir infrastructure is anchor-only and unresolved.

components.label: The lightly occupied matrix (C013, C014, C020, C021, C022, C029)
components.note: The river-distance gradient (E010) and the fourteen-region phytolith synthesis (E011) are admitted; the modelling that fixes proportion and the critiques that would discount the negatives are held on anchors alone. The matrix density itself is unmeasured.

components.label: The disappearance on Carvajal's reaches (C010, C015, C023)
components.note: Collapse of 62–88 percent by mixed mechanisms is documented for upper-Amazon provinces (E008) and no pre-contact crash shows at basin scale (E020); the Solimões has no reconstruction and the fade-out mechanism is anchor-only.

researchPriority.reason: Two desk items (the corridor test, the manuscript-witness table) and one archival reading (the 1650 Omagua headcount) could move the founding question decisively at low cost; the matrix-density and erasure-calibration items decide the mosaic-versus-modest-skeptic proportion that the record cannot yet fix; and the anchor of the earthwork leg is a founder-funded paper weeks old, which makes independent calibration urgent.

claimAssessments.reasoning: The claim states what the chronicle describes, not whether it was true. Denevan's manuscript comparison (E005, E006) and Lopes's verbatim quotations (E007) quote the text; E006 qualifies the picture toward sporadic bluff settlement, which is the very alternation of populated and empty reaches the claim records.

treatment.plainLanguage: Carvajal wrote that he saw crowded towns, food stores, roads and organized chiefdoms along long stretches of river, with empty stretches between.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: What the friar said is not in dispute; whether it was true is the case. Its alternating pattern turns the account into a testable spatial prediction rather than a slogan, but the text itself decides nothing.
treatment.strongestObjection: A chronicle's content tells us nothing about the world until corroborated, and even ‘what he said’ has edges: the text survives in two branches that differ.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A witness table (AMZ-R002) showing the qualitative descriptions, not just the figures, are branch-specific
Evidence that Oviedo's redaction introduced settlement descriptions Carvajal did not write

claimAssessments.reasoning: E005 (strong) quotes Denevan's branch comparison verbatim: the 50,000/10,000/8,000 figures and the four-to-five-league villages are absent from Oviedo, which keeps one figure of about 5,000. Verified from an OCR copy; no page-level collation yet.

treatment.plainLanguage: The biggest numbers in Carvajal's story are only in one family of manuscripts; the other family tells the same crowded story with much smaller figures.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Separates the world from the arithmetic: the inflation sits in transmission, which cuts against invention (the eyewitness picture is stable) and against any account that spends the figures as counts.
treatment.strongestObjection: Absence from Oviedo does not prove Carvajal never wrote the figures — Oviedo may have abridged them — and the comparison is one geographer's, verified from a scan rather than collated page by page.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A page-level collation placing the extreme figures in both witnesses
Evidence that Oviedo systematically cut numbers from the text he inserted

claimAssessments.reasoning: E007 (strong) quotes Lopes et al. verbatim on Nunes's 1538 entry into Machiparo and the ten Ursúa accounts of 1560 describing dense settlement, infinite maize stores, Inca-like roads without walls and renowned ceramics on the middle Solimões. The record's own limits: Nunes survives as a 1553/54 letter in a modern edition; fortifications are not among the shared features.

treatment.plainLanguage: Other Europeans who saw the same stretch of river in 1538 and 1560 described the same kind of crowded, road-connected world, without Carvajal's giant numbers.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Convergence on mundane detail by witnesses for different crowns is what invention cannot produce; it is the record that most decides against the first account. It corroborates the corridors only, not the basin.
treatment.strongestObjection: All the witnesses travelled the same richest corridor and wrote in the same conquest-narrative genre with shared incentives to describe wealth; independence is Lopes's characterization, and the primaries have not been read here.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Reading the Nunes letter and Ursúa accounts and finding textual dependence on Carvajal
A corridor test (AMZ-R001) returning no contact-horizon settlement on the Machiparo reaches

claimAssessments.reasoning: E001 (strong) quotes the 432 documented earthworks, the 183,000 km² circumscription and the 24,000–30,000 projection verbatim; E003 dates the peak to AD 100–300; E038/E039 set a basin-wide model beside it as context, showing several-fold divergence between published totals.

treatment.plainLanguage: Lasers flown over the forest found hundreds of ancient earthworks where satellites saw few, and the team projects tens of thousands across one region of the southwest.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Decisive against ecological impossibility; weak about 1542, since the florescence is a millennium earlier and far from Carvajal's route. The projection is a block extrapolation.
treatment.strongestObjection: The 24,000–30,000 figure is extrapolated from sampled densities, exceeds a basin-wide model's total for all Amazonia, and the study was funded by this site's founder.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A probability-stratified blind LiDAR sample (AMZ-R006) finding densities far below the regional projection
A redefinition of earthwork classes that removes most of the 432 from the count

claimAssessments.reasoning: E002 (strong) quotes both the 1.25–3 million derivation and the paper's own single-family alternative of 250,000–600,000 (315,000–760,000 with canopy correction). The sensitivity is the authors'; the emphasis is this case's.

treatment.plainLanguage: The headline population for the ancient earthwork region depends on guesses about how many monuments were in use at once and how many people each needed; change the guesses and the number shrinks fivefold.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Decides against treating any published total as a measurement, which is the garden-Amazon account's weakest joint; it says nothing about whether the corridors were real.
treatment.strongestObjection: The authors label the single-family reading very unlikely; displaying the full envelope rather than their preferred figure is an editorial choice.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Household-size archaeology at Aquiry mounds fixing persons per monument
A dependency-corrected re-derivation (AMZ-R004) narrowing the envelope

claimAssessments.reasoning: E004 (strong) quotes the AD 1250–1500 dating of fortified villages along 1,800 km and the population derivation with its stated assumptions of contemporaneity, ethnographic formulae and MaxEnt extrapolation.

treatment.plainLanguage: Along the southern edge of the Amazon, people were living in fortified earthwork villages in the two and a half centuries before Europeans arrived.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Contact-era fortified settlement at regional scale is an existence proof against invention and against a purely modest reading; but the southern rim is not the Solimões, and the half-million-to-million figure is a model.
treatment.strongestObjection: The population rests on every site being occupied at once, and the arc lies far from Carvajal's route.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Re-dating showing the villages were sequential rather than contemporaneous
A corridor test null on Carvajal's reaches, which would leave the southern rim an isolated hotspot

claimAssessments.reasoning: E014 (strong) quotes the drainage canals, savannah farm ponds and 178-sample phytolith record of ubiquitous maize; the record's limitation notes the Casarabe florescence ends around 1400.

treatment.plainLanguage: One Bolivian savanna culture drained and watered its landscape to grow maize all year — direct evidence that intensive farming was possible.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Answers the subsistence-impossibility argument that underwrote the invention account; it does not describe 1542 or the forested corridors Carvajal saw.
treatment.strongestObjection: One culture on one savanna, ended a century and a half before Orellana; the terra-firme forest is a different environment.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Phytolith re-analysis attributing the maize signal to later or non-agricultural deposition
Evidence that Casarabe collapsed from resource failure, which would sharpen rather than remove the limits reading

claimAssessments.reasoning: E012 (moderate) and E040/E041 (moderate, same research network) support the domesticated-tree concentration; E013 qualifies it with the post-Columbian confound; dark earths and raised fields are directly documented in E017, E015 and E016.

treatment.plainLanguage: People reshaped Amazonian ground for centuries — dark soils, raised fields, forest islands, and orchards of useful trees around old settlements.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Establishes long engineering; the tree signal cannot separate pre- from post-Columbian management, so it weighs less for the pre-contact picture than it seems.
treatment.strongestObjection: Five post-Columbian centuries likely shaped the observed tree patterns more than pre-Columbian ones (E013), and the corroborating study shares authors and species list with the original.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Dated stratigraphy showing domesticated-species surges post-1500 at the sites in question
Independent species lists and teams reproducing the association

claimAssessments.reasoning: E016 (strong) dates intermittent raised-field use from AD 570–770 in a few construction events; E015 (moderate) proposes flood-risk mitigation where no alternatives existed. Bermeo-area fields only.

treatment.plainLanguage: Some famous raised fields were built in bursts during flood-prone periods, not farmed continuously as a permanent breadbasket.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Cuts against reading every earthwork as intensive, continuous farmland — the garden Amazon's inference — without touching the corridors.
treatment.strongestObjection: One field complex studied in detail; other complexes may have been used differently.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Dating at other raised-field complexes showing continuous use
Palaeohydrological evidence decoupling construction events from flood episodes

claimAssessments.reasoning: E008 (strong) quotes Newson's Table 1 declines (88 percent Napo–Aguarico, 62–64 percent Mainas by circa 1700) and the mixed-mechanism passages including flight from exposed river locations. Upper-Amazon provinces with mission records only.

treatment.plainLanguage: Where colonial records allow counting, whole provinces lost two-thirds to nine-tenths of their people within about 150 years, through disease, raids, missions, forced labor, revolt and flight.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Supplies the murdered-world account with a documented mechanism and magnitude, and one that empties riverbanks specifically; its reach to the Solimões is extrapolation.
treatment.strongestObjection: The provinces counted are upper-Amazon mission regions, and the contact-period baselines are themselves reconstructions.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Province-by-province timelines (AMZ-R005) showing modest decline on the Solimões
Revision of the contact-period baselines downward

claimAssessments.reasoning: E017 (strong) dates Belterra Plateau sites AD 1300 to seventeenth-century colonization with dark earths, ponds and roads; E018 (strong) dates Cacoal AD 1300–1650; E019 (moderate, journalism) gives Xingu occupation to 1770 in layouts matching living Kuikuro villages.

treatment.plainLanguage: Several large settlement systems were still inhabited when Europeans arrived and after — some by the ancestors of communities living there now.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Contact-era complexity is the direct refutation of invention and the strongest check on a purely modest reading; the gap is geographic, since these lie downstream and south of Carvajal's famous reaches.
treatment.strongestObjection: None of these systems is on the Machiparo or Omagua reaches, and the Xingu dates rest on a news feature pending primary reports.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Primary Xingu reports contradicting the 1770 end date or the layout continuity
Re-dating that ends Belterra or Marajó occupation before 1500

claimAssessments.reasoning: E009 (decisive) quotes Denevan rejecting his own habitat-density method for the 5.1–6.8 million figure while still holding 5–6 million reasonable on other grounds.

treatment.plainLanguage: The famous population totals are models sharing assumptions, and the leading estimator publicly disowned the method behind his own number while keeping the number.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Decides against reading the spread of published totals as competing measurements; it does not tell us which total is right.
treatment.strongestObjection: Denevan still defends the order of magnitude, so an expert judgment for millions survives the method's failure.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A dependency-corrected re-derivation (AMZ-R004) showing independent method families converge on one range

claimAssessments.reasoning: E010 (strong) quotes the 7,363-site model: distance from river is the top predictor (21.5 percent permutation importance) and interfluves were more sparsely populated. Site databases inherit survey-effort bias.

treatment.plainLanguage: Across thousands of known sites, being near a river is the best predictor of ancient occupation; the deep forest between rivers is much sparser.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: The main quantitative check on the garden Amazon and the spine of the mosaic's matrix half; it cannot say how sparse, because archaeologists survey where they can reach.
treatment.strongestObjection: The gradient may partly measure where surveys have gone rather than where people lived.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Promise-blind interfluve surveys (AMZ-R003) finding densities comparable to riverine ones

claimAssessments.reasoning: E011 (strong) quotes the cumulative fourteen-region synthesis finding little to no evidence of annual crops, clearing, anthropic soils, tree enrichment or recurrent fire in most sampled terra firme. The record's own limitations note sparse coring and that negatives count only where the proxy could detect the activity; the formal sampling critique (C021) is anchor-only.

treatment.plainLanguage: Where soils in the western and between-river Amazon have been cored, most show closed forest with little sign of farming or burning before Europeans.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Caps the garden Amazon directly; low bearing on Carvajal's corridors, which it does not sample. Its weight depends on how far erasure and thin sampling discount a negative.
treatment.strongestObjection: Negative evidence is bounded by proxy sensitivity, sparse sampling and time-graded erasure — arguments the ledger holds only as statements so far.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Promise-blind gridded coring (AMZ-R003) finding intensive-use signals in the interfluves
Erasure calibration (AMZ-R008) showing signals vanish within four centuries

claimAssessments.reasoning: E020 (moderate) quotes the logistic fit over 1,700 years and the authors' attribution of the terminal decline to sampling bias compounded by post-contact collapse. Summed radiocarbon distributions proxy relative change with stated biases.

treatment.plainLanguage: Dated remains across the basin suggest populations were still growing toward a ceiling when Europeans arrived, not already declining.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Weighs against an endogenous pre-contact crash as an alternative to the murdered-world timing; says nothing about how many people the ceiling held.
treatment.strongestObjection: Radiocarbon sums are aggregate proxies with taphonomic and sampling biases, and ‘carrying capacity (however high)’ is a shape, not a number.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Regional radiocarbon series showing pre-contact declines on the corridors
Demonstration that the logistic shape is a sampling artefact

claimAssessments.reasoning: This synthesis claim has no anchor and no evidence record of its own; it is graded on the admitted records for its named dependencies — E001, E004, E014, E017, E018, E019 for dense engineered corridors and hotspots; E010 and E011 for a lighter matrix. Both halves are directly evidenced; the magnitude in ‘much more lightly occupied’ is inferred, not measured, and the qualifiers that would sharpen it (C020, C021, C022, C029) are anchor-only.

treatment.plainLanguage: The Amazon before contact was patchy: crowded, engineered places along rivers and savannas, with much emptier forest between.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: It is the mosaic account itself; it rules out wilderness and wall-to-wall civilization but does not fix the proportion that separates the mosaic from the modest skeptic.
treatment.strongestObjection: Heterogeneity is close to a truism; the load-bearing part — how light the matrix was — is exactly what no admitted record measures.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Promise-blind interfluve surveys (AMZ-R003) in either direction
A corridor test (AMZ-R001) showing Carvajal's populated reaches no denser than matched controls

claimAssessments.reasoning: Rests on E007 (independent witnesses), E005 (branch-specific figures) and E006 (bluff geography) through C001–C003; E003 qualifies it by dating the Aquiry peak a millennium earlier; E077 (weak, context) records a geographic-route assessment of trustworthiness that is silent on the qualitative-versus-numerical split. The contact-era systems in C006 and C011 lie off his route, and the corridor test is unrun.

treatment.plainLanguage: Carvajal probably told the truth about the kind of world he saw and cannot be trusted on the huge numbers.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: This is the founding question's answer; it separates the murdered-world and mosaic readings from invention and marks where the modest skeptic still has room.
treatment.strongestObjection: Every corroboration is either the same corridor and genre, archaeologically off his route, or a thousand years too early; nothing dated to 1400–1650 has yet been placed on his populated reaches.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: The corridor test (AMZ-R001) in either direction
A witness table (AMZ-R002) showing the qualitative descriptions are branch-specific
The 1650 Omagua headcount (AMZ-R007) fixing how populated his reach still was a century later

claimAssessments.reasoning: E021 (moderate) documents Pärssinen and Ranzi in the 2024 series cast; the first-party anchor states the seven-chapter coverage. Genealogy only; carries no weight for any empirical claim.

treatment.plainLanguage: A popular author championed the Acre earthworks and their researchers years before the 2026 results reached mainstream attention.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Decides nothing about the Amazon; recorded so the genealogy of the question is truthful.
treatment.strongestObjection: Who kept a question alive is irrelevant to whether its answer is true, in either direction.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Evidence the book's Amazon coverage was not as stated
Nothing about the Amazon itself would move this claim

claimAssessments.reasoning: Held on its anchor alone: the ledger knows where the weir, causeway and pond findings are stated and has admitted no evidence record from the source; the anchored line is the authors' postulate about function. E022 on the child claim documents fish consumption, not the infrastructure.

treatment.plainLanguage: A study reports that ancient people built zigzag weirs and ponds across a Bolivian floodplain to trap fish; this record has not yet admitted the observation behind that report.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: If admitted, landscape-scale fisheries would answer the protein objection directly; as an anchor-only statement it carries no weight.
treatment.strongestObjection: No admitted observation; the anchor quotes a postulate about function, not a measurement.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Admission of evidence records from the San Joaquín study on the weir geometry and pond distribution
Faunal evidence that the ponds held trapped fish

claimAssessments.reasoning: E022 (strong) quotes more than 17,000 fish remains at Loma Salvatierra, 50 km from the Mamoré, occupied AD 500–1400, with dry-season small-water species named. One site; the source notes a paucity of large river fish.

treatment.plainLanguage: One ancient mound far from the big river is full of fish bones from all seasons — people ate from local waters year-round.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: An existence proof against the year-round-protein objection; one site is not a census and the occupation ends before contact.
treatment.strongestObjection: A single interfluvial mound in a savanna, not the forested terra firme most of the sparse-Amazon argument concerns.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Faunal assemblages at other interfluvial mounds showing seasonal abandonment
Re-identification of the dry-season species

claimAssessments.reasoning: Held on its anchor alone: the ‘limited, albeit impressive’ phrase and the two-thirds figure are located in the source's text but no evidence record has been admitted. The model is also built from the same access-biased site base as E010.

treatment.plainLanguage: A machine-learning study is reported to find that spectacular earthworks and dark earths cover a limited fraction of the basin, with humbler sites dominating most of it — a statement this record holds without an admitted observation.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: A rung of the modest-skeptic account on proportion; if admitted it would weight the matrix toward humbler occupation, not emptiness.
treatment.strongestObjection: No admitted record; and a prediction over biased known sites inherits their bias.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Admission of an evidence record from the study with the predicted extents
Promise-blind surveys (AMZ-R003) measuring site-type proportions directly

claimAssessments.reasoning: Held on its anchor alone: the reply's sampling arithmetic is located but no evidence record has been admitted. It bears on C014 as a critique, and C014's own record already notes sparse coring.

treatment.plainLanguage: Critics say the ‘empty west’ conclusion rests on a cubic meter of soil from five spots standing in for two million square kilometers — a critique this record holds as a statement, not yet as a record.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: If admitted, it discounts the fourteen-region negatives and favors the mosaic or garden readings over the modest skeptic; as a statement it moves nothing.
treatment.strongestObjection: No admitted record; and the critique's own count (300 cores, five clusters) may not describe the fourteen-region synthesis as of 2024.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Admission of the reply's evidence record
A tally of the actual coring effort behind the 2024 synthesis

claimAssessments.reasoning: Held on its anchor alone: the erasure sentence is located but no evidence record has been admitted. Separately admitted records on C061 and C062 (E073, E074) date the erased Upano occupation to 300–600 CE with reoccupation to 1200 CE, so even if admitted the claim speaks to a signal at least a millennium old.

treatment.plainLanguage: A study of one Ecuadorian valley reports that forest regrowth wiped out the ecological traces of ancient occupation while later colonial traces survived — a report this ledger holds without an admitted record.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: It would discount palaeoecological negatives for old occupations; the dated Upano chronology shows the erased signal was a thousand years old, which limits how far it can discount contact-era negatives four centuries old.
treatment.strongestObjection: No admitted record, and the one dated case is not analogous in age to a riverbank depopulated in the 1600s.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Admission of the Upano palaeoecology record
Erasure calibration (AMZ-R008) showing four-century-old signals also vanish

claimAssessments.reasoning: Held on its anchor alone: the ‘fade outs’ phrase is located in Newson 2003 but no evidence record has been admitted for it. E008 on C010, from the same source, documents mixed mechanisms and flight but not the fade-out proposition.

treatment.plainLanguage: The idea that epidemics died out in thin populations and were repeatedly reintroduced by raids and missions is stated in the source this record cites, but the observation behind it has not been admitted.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: If admitted, it explains how collapse could be late and interactive on the Solimões, helping the murdered-world timing; as a statement it carries no weight.
treatment.strongestObjection: No admitted record; the mechanism is drawn from upper-Amazon provinces.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Admission of Newson's fade-out passage as an evidence record
Solimões timelines (AMZ-R005) showing a single early wave instead

claimAssessments.reasoning: Held on its anchor alone: the ‘almost 80 percent at 0–1 percent probability’ passage was declined at intake because the quoted span was not found verbatim, and no evidence record has been admitted. The same source's admitted records (E038, E039) give the undiscovered total and the Acre rectangle, not this figure.

treatment.plainLanguage: A basin-wide model is reported to give most of Amazonia almost no chance of holding an earthwork; this ledger has not verified that figure in the paper's text.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: If admitted, it is the sharpest quantitative statement of the modest-skeptic and mosaic matrix; unverified, it decides nothing.
treatment.strongestObjection: The quote could not be located verbatim, and the model corrects for observability with a modelled correction.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Locating the passage in the published text and admitting it
A stratified blind LiDAR sample (AMZ-R006) testing the low-probability stratum

claimAssessments.reasoning: E073 (strong) quotes the excavating team's dating of the Upano occupation from around 500 BCE to between 300 and 600 CE, from an author-accepted manuscript with almost seventy radiocarbon dates per its supplement; the revised sequence is promised in a later paper.

treatment.plainLanguage: The people who built the Upano Valley platforms lived there from about 2,500 years ago until roughly 1,400–1,700 years ago.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Fixes the age of the signal the Upano erasure argument (C022) says was lost, and shows Upano is not contact-era evidence; it does not bear on Carvajal's reaches.
treatment.strongestObjection: The end date is a range from an author manuscript, and later Huapula reoccupation (C062) blurs when the valley was last modified.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A revised radiocarbon sequence moving the end of occupation substantially
Evidence of continuous occupation into the second millennium

claimAssessments.reasoning: E072 (weak) records the abstract's statement that the article verifies Carvajal's account through its geographic reference points and finds the manuscript a trustworthy source; the body was not read, so the route argument is unverified.

treatment.plainLanguage: A 2018 scholarly article, checking Carvajal's geography against the river, concludes the manuscript is trustworthy — known here only from its abstract.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Convergence by a different route on Carvajal's general credibility; it says nothing about the numbers or the qualitative-versus-numerical split, so it barely moves C017 (E077, context).
treatment.strongestObjection: An abstract's verdict without its argument; geographic plausibility of a route does not vouch for what the traveler said he saw along it.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Reading the body and finding the route argument fails or contradicts other identifications
Evidence the geographic consistency is shared by the branch carrying the extreme figures only
